newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to join lucrative Korean nuclear group.
newsitem.headline: EU to join lucrative Korean nuclear group.

text.p: European Union companies should soon be able to compete for millions of dollars of contracts in a North Korean power plant following a deal on Thursday on the terms of EU membership of the scheme's executive board.

A spokesman for EU Trade Commissioner Leon Brittan said the Commission had initialled a deal of "enormous political and financial significance", setting out the terms of EU membership of the Korean Peninsula Energy Development Organisation (KEDO).
"It shows for the first time that we do not only have a commercial interest in East-Asia but a strategic interest to promote peace and security there," spokesman Peter Guilford told a news briefing.

KEDO was set up two years ago by the United States, Japan and South Korea to help North Korea develop its nuclear energy industry while at the same time ensuring its reactors are not diverted to non-energy activities.

"Active involvement in KEDO...will also create opportunities for EU companies to compete for KEDO projects in a fair and open industrial tendering process," Brittan said in a statement welcoming the provisional deal, which will now be submitted to EU foreign ministers for formal approval.

Stephen Bosworth, KEDO's executive director, has said the EU's proposed contribution of 75 million ecus ($86 million) over five years to the five-billion-dollar international scheme will make European companies eligible to bid for contracts "worth substantially more".

In exchange for western aid to build two lightwater reactors by 2003 and supply Pyongyang with 500,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil a year until then, North Korea will dismantle two partially built heavywater reactors.

The EU has spent five million ecus this year on the project and EU governments are expected to ask the European Parliament -- which shares control over the EU budget with member states -- to approve the release of a further 10 million by December.
But members of the parliament last week criticised the plan.

Instead of using EU money to muscle in on a 2,000 megawatt commercial project which would otherwise be controlled by its competitors, the 15-member EU bloc should spend the 10-million- ecu reserve to help stem the famine sweeping North Korea, German Green Euro-MP Undine von Blottnitz told reporters.
Commission spokesman Joao Vale de Almeida told reporters on Thursday the EU executive hoped to announce a famine aid package on Friday.
Australia, New Zealand, Canada, Chile, Indonesia and Finland are general members of KEDO without a voice on its executive board.
